text.en: Meena shouted in an empty hall and heard her voice come back. "Sound reflects," said her teacher.

Sound travelling through air or water forms longitudinal waves. Wave velocity is the distance the wave travels in unit time, and V = n x wavelength, where n is the frequency. Sound usually travels faster in everyday solids than in liquids and gases. Its speed depends on the stiffness and density of the medium.
Sound reflects from a surface following the laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A separate echo usually requires around 0.1 second of delay, corresponding to a wall about 17 m away at 340 m/s. Echoes are used to measure the depth of the sea and the speed of sound. The ear trumpet, megaphone and sound board use reflection.
The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency of sound due to relative motion between the source and the listener. The pitch rises as the source approaches and falls as it moves away. Doppler ultrasound uses sound to study motion. Doppler radar uses a similar frequency shift of radio waves.
Sound travelling through air or water is a longitudinal wave. The particles move back and forth along the direction in which the sound travels.
Wave velocity is the distance the wave travels in unit time, and V = n x wavelength, where n is the frequency.
Sound usually travels faster in everyday solids than in liquids and gases. Its speed depends on both the stiffness and the density of the medium.
Sound reflects from a surface following the laws of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

A separate echo is usually heard if the reflected sound arrives about one tenth of a second later. At about three hundred and forty metres per second in air, that corresponds to a reflector about seventeen metres away.
Echoes are used to measure the depth of the sea and the speed of sound.
The ear trumpet, megaphone and sound board use reflection.
The Doppler effect is the apparent change in the frequency of sound due to relative motion between the source and the listener.
Pluck a string. Its back-and-forth movement disturbs the nearby air. Those disturbances pass outwards as a sound wave.
When the source moves forward, it pushes nearby air particles closer. This region of higher pressure is a compression.
When the source moves the other way a lower-pressure region can follow. A train of compressions and rarefactions travels through the air.
The air particles vibrate near their normal positions. The wave can travel far without the same particles travelling from the source to your ear.

board.text: Matter moves locally; the disturbance moves on

text.en: A vacuum has no particles to transfer these vibrations. Sound can travel in air, water or a suitable solid.
A vibration with frequency two hundred hertz completes two hundred cycles every second. Higher frequency generally gives a higher pitch.
A larger vibration amplitude usually means a louder sound at the same distance. Loudness can change even when frequency and pitch stay the same.
Measure from the centre of one compression to the centre of the next compression. That distance is the wavelength.

board.text: Wavelength is one complete spatial cycle

text.en: A wave with frequency two hundred hertz and wavelength one point seven metres travels three hundred and forty metres per second.
Warm air generally carries sound faster than colder air. Use the speed given in a calculation if it differs from the approximate value.
Sounds above the upper limit are called ultrasound. Sounds below the lower limit are called infrasound. The exact limits vary with the listener.

board.text: Human hearing is roughly 20 Hz to 20 kHz

text.en: When a wave reaches a wall, some of it can return to the room. The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence measured from the normal.

board.text: Reflection sends part of the sound back

text.en: Curtains or absorbent panels reduce reflections in a room. This helps keep repeated reflections from muddying speech.

board.text: Soft surfaces can absorb some sound

text.en: An echo is a distinct repeat. Reflections arriving very close together can blend with the original to produce reverberation.
Sound goes from the source to the wall and back to the listener. If source and listener are together, the round trip covers twice the wall distance.

board.text: The echo path has two legs

text.en: A wall echo returning in two tenths of a second at three hundred and forty metres per second comes from thirty-four metres away.
A ship can send a sound pulse towards the seabed and measure the return time. Use the speed of sound in water and halve the round-trip distance.
The source moves closer between pulses. In front of it the pulses are closer together, and a stationary listener hears a higher frequency.
As the source moves away, successive pulses take longer to reach the listener. The received frequency is lower.
A listener moving towards a stationary sound source meets wavefronts more often. Moving away gives fewer arrivals per second.
A steady whistle can sound higher as it approaches and lower after it passes. What changes is how often waves reach you.

board.text: Doppler change does not require a changing source frequency

text.en: Use travel time and wave speed for echoes. Use changes in wavefront arrival rate for Doppler shifts.

board.text: Choose the model that answers the question

problem.en: A sound of frequency 500 Hz has wavelength 0.68 m. Find its speed.

text.en: V = n x wavelength.
Speed = 340 m/s.

problem.en: Sound travels through air at 340 m/s with frequency 170 Hz. Find its wavelength.

text.en: Rearrange v = fλ to λ = v/f.

why.en: The wave travels one wavelength in each cycle.
Speed divided by cycles per second yields metres per cycle.

problem.en: An echo returns 0.30 s after a clap. Estimate the wall distance at 340 m/s.

text.en: The sound travels a total of 340 × 0.30 = 102 m.

why.en: This includes the outgoing and returning journeys.

text.en: The wall is 51 m away.

why.en: The distance to the wall is half the round trip.

problem.en: A stationary listener hears an approaching train give a higher pitch. Did its whistle necessarily change?

text.en: No. The whistle can vibrate at a steady frequency.

why.en: The source moves closer to the listener between pulses.

text.en: The listener receives wavefronts more frequently.

why.en: The higher heard pitch is a Doppler shift.

prompt.en: A friend says The Doppler effect changes the speed of sound. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: It changes the apparent frequency, not the speed.

points.en: Echo needs at least 0.1 s gap.
